source: Pleiss, Schiffer, von Weizsaecker (2026) Disentangling generalization and memorization in large language models using chess
finding: Closest LLM analogue of the Chase and Simon contrast: well-known opening positions versus random boards. LLM chess skill falls steeply as familiar patterns thin out.
numbers: 500 positions per condition (1,500 total). Random boards: 10 pieces per side placed at random. Across GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, GPT-5, average centipawn loss was 4.75x higher near-distribution and 7.79x higher on random boards than on familiar positions.
limits: Task is choosing a move, not recalling a position. Familiarity is estimated from Lichess Masters counts (at least 1,000 occurrences), not from known training data. Random boards have 20 pieces, unlike Chase-Simon shuffles of real positions.
agent_relevance: Strong sign that LLM skill is pattern-bound like human chunk-bound skill. A subgoal library should help mainly on familiar problem classes.

source: Pleiss, Schiffer, von Weizsaecker (2026) Disentangling generalization and memorization in large language models using chess
finding: Illegal-move rate rises as positions lose familiar structure, although the rules are the same everywhere.
numbers: Illegal moves overall: GPT-3.5 74.7%, GPT-4o 41.6%, GPT-5 33.8%. Rate 1.46x higher near-distribution and 4.72x higher on random boards than on familiar ones. Claude Opus 4.6: 0.2% illegal (familiar), 8.2% (near), 51.6% (random). Gemini 3 Flash: 2.2%, 17.0%, 72.0%.
limits: One prompt format per model. Claude and Gemini queried March 2026.
agent_relevance: Rule use fails when chunk retrieval fails. Legality and constraint checks should sit outside the model's pattern memory, as an explicit verify step.

source: Pleiss, Schiffer, von Weizsaecker (2026) Disentangling generalization and memorization in large language models using chess
finding: On random boards base models do no better than random legal play, even with illegal moves removed.
numbers: GPT-5 on familiar positions: centipawn loss 26.19 (SD 49.53), about 4x better than random legal moves. On random boards no base model beat random play. Gains per generation in centipawn loss on random boards: 9.08% (GPT-3.5 to 4o) and 5.73% (4o to 5); on familiar positions 70.7% and 69.92%.
limits: Same caveats as c01. Reasoning mode tested only on GPT-5.
agent_relevance: Scale mostly adds chunks, not better search from scratch. A scaffold cannot count on the model improvising outside what it has stored.

source: Pleiss, Schiffer, von Weizsaecker (2026) Disentangling generalization and memorization in large language models using chess
finding: Extra reasoning helps, but helps least where chunks are missing.
numbers: GPT-5 minimal vs moderate reasoning effort: centipawn loss fell 71.74% overall (85.3% near, 77.25% familiar, 64.69% random). Per 1,000 reasoning tokens the relative gain was 22.55% familiar, 7.23% near, 3.81% random.
limits: Single model family. Gain per token is relative, so baseline differences matter.
agent_relevance: Test-time compute pays most when relevant stored patterns exist. Pair thinking steps with a retrievable library, not tokens alone.

source: Pleiss, Schiffer, von Weizsaecker (2026) Disentangling generalization and memorization in large language models using chess
finding: Newer models improve fastest where positions are familiar and slowest on novel ones.
numbers: Illegal-move drop by generation: 44.31% (GPT-3.5 to 4o), 18.75% (4o to 5). Centipawn-loss reduction: 33.12%, then 14.23%.
limits: Three OpenAI generations plus one Claude and one Gemini snapshot.
agent_relevance: Part of scale gain is coverage. The scaffold's job is the novel part.

source: Bennett and Gobet (2025) Automatic adaptation to concept complexity and subjective natural concepts: a cognitive model based on chunking (CogAct)
finding: CogAct is a chunking model in the CHREST and EPAM line. It learns concepts from raw text, music and chess with the same mechanisms and no domain-specific features.
numbers: Chess opening classification (French vs Sicilian): 53 of 61 correct (chance 31), about 85%. Literature 41 of 60 (chance 10). Music 42 of 60 (chance 15). Long-term memory grew to about 3,000 chess chunks, 34,000 literature chunks, 22,000 music chunks.
limits: Simulation, no human data; preprint. Authors note experts need far more chunks than the model had. Author-level categories were a weak point.
agent_relevance: A chunk store with one activation rule can classify across domains. A subgoal library could use similarity-based activation instead of hand-built keys.

source: Bennett and Gobet (2025) Automatic adaptation to concept complexity and subjective natural concepts: a cognitive model based on chunking (CogAct)
finding: CogAct matched the older CHREST result on chess, which needed hand-crafted chess features from a master-level player.
numbers: About 85% for both CHREST and CogAct on French vs Sicilian (Lane and Gobet 2012 for CHREST). CogAct used no chess-specific feature detectors.
limits: Small test set (57 to 61 positions). Authors' own report.
agent_relevance: Dropping hand-built domain features without losing accuracy suggests generic chunk learning may be enough for an agent library.

source: Bennett and Gobet (2025) Automatic adaptation to concept complexity and subjective natural concepts: a cognitive model based on chunking (CogAct)
finding: Authors compare chunking to deep learning: one activation formula works for chunks and for neural units, and both fit human music-categorisation data at broadly similar levels.
numbers: Activation formula interchangeable between CogAct and the ANN baseline. The ANN could not adapt its size to concept complexity, CogAct could. No fit figures taken from the passage read.
limits: ANN baseline was meant as illustration, not state of the art. Argument is partly theoretical.
agent_relevance: Text chunks and learned weights may be two views of one thing. A text library is an inspectable layer over the model's own patterns.

source: Bennett and Gobet (2025) Automatic adaptation to concept complexity and subjective natural concepts: a cognitive model based on chunking (CogAct)
finding: Secondhand scale figure for human experts: over 300,000 long-term chess chunks (Gobet and Simon 1998; Richman et al. 1996).
numbers: 300,000+ chunks for master level, versus about 3,000 chess chunks in CogAct.
limits: Via this paper. The original studies were not opened.
agent_relevance: Experts hold very many small chunks, not a handful of big plans. Favour many small library entries.

source: Bennett and Gobet (2025) Automatic adaptation to concept complexity and subjective natural concepts: a cognitive model based on chunking (CogAct)
finding: The paper runs no LLM on chunking tasks. It notes GPT-4 can still blunder on simple arithmetic and suggests large training data may reduce the bias-variance trade-off.
numbers: Not quantitative.
limits: Footnote-level remark, citing Bubeck et al. 2023.
agent_relevance: No direct LLM test of CHREST or EPAM predictions was found in the sources opened.

source: Voyager: An open-ended embodied agent with large language models (Wang et al. 2023)
finding: Voyager stores working programs as skills in a library that GPT-4 retrieves. This is chunking at the code level: new skills build on older ones.
numbers: 63 unique items in 160 prompting iterations (3.3x prior best). Wooden tools 15.3x faster, stone 8.5x, iron 6.4x. Only agent to reach diamond tools. Travelled 2.3x farther.
limits: Baselines (AutoGPT, ReAct, Reflexion) lacked the curriculum, so gains mix curriculum and library.
agent_relevance: Direct precedent for a subgoal library of chunks. The unit is a verified, executable, named skill.

source: Voyager (Wang et al. 2023)
finding: Ablation: without the skill library progress plateaus late; a random curriculum cuts discovered items by 93%.
numbers: No-library variant 'tends to plateau in the later stages'. Random curriculum: 93% fewer items. Exact library-ablation counts sit in a figure and were not read as numbers.
limits: Library effect reported qualitatively in the text read.
agent_relevance: Library value grows with horizon. Expect small gains on short tasks, larger on long ones. Ablate the library in our runs.

source: Buffer of Thoughts (Yang et al. 2024)
finding: Buffer of Thoughts distils high-level thought templates from solved problems, stores them in a meta-buffer and retrieves one for a new problem. A template is a chunk of reasoning, not of facts.
numbers: Game of 24: GPT-4 3.0%, ToT 74.0%, meta-prompting 67.0%, BoT 82.4%. Reported gains over the prior best: 11% Game of 24, 20% Geometric Shapes, 51% Checkmate-in-One. Cost about 12% of multi-query methods.
limits: Authors' own benchmarks, GPT-4 base. Table values read from text extraction.
agent_relevance: Closest published method to a template library inside an LLM loop.

source: Buffer of Thoughts (Yang et al. 2024)
finding: Ablations: removing the meta-buffer hurts. With a buffer-manager that adds templates over time, accuracy climbs round after round; without it, it stays flat.
numbers: Four rounds of 50 random questions per benchmark. With buffer-manager accuracy rises each round and time falls; without it no upward trend. Meta-buffer ablation lowers accuracy on Llama3-70B and GPT-4 (bars in a figure).
limits: Small rounds (50 per benchmark), no seed spread shown.
agent_relevance: Library growth is a learning curve with no weight update. Log library size against accuracy.

source: Agent Workflow Memory (Wang et al. 2024)
finding: AWM induces reusable workflows (chunks of action steps) from past trajectories and keeps them in memory. Works offline from examples and online from its own successes.
numbers: WebArena: +12.0 absolute points, 51.1% relative success rate over the BrowserGym baseline (gpt-4). About 2.0 fewer steps per example than Autoeval. Mind2Web: 24.6% relative step-success gain. As train-test gaps widen: +8.9 to +14.0 points over baselines.
limits: Web navigation only. Online mode needs an automatic success judge.
agent_relevance: Abstracted workflows transfer across tasks and sites, with larger gains as train and test differ more.

source: DreamCoder (Ellis et al. 2020)
finding: Wake-sleep library learning compresses repeated sub-programs into new named primitives and trains a search guide. Chunking as description-length compression.
numbers: SyGuS text editing: before learning 3.7% solved in 10 min (mean 235 s); after 79.6% (mean 40 s). Best competition solver CVC4 82.4% with 1 hour and 8 CPUs; DreamCoder 84.3% with that budget. Learned about 20 list routines.
limits: Small domain languages. Library built by symbolic compression, not by an LLM.
agent_relevance: Explains why a library helps: it shortens solution depth. Keep a library item only if it shortens real solutions.

source: LILO (Grand et al. 2024)
finding: LILO swaps DreamCoder's enumerative search for LLM synthesis plus Stitch compression. Naming and documenting abstractions (AutoDoc) was needed for the LLM to use them.
numbers: LLM Solver with no library beats DreamCoder by +32.20 on REGEX. LILO beats DreamCoder: +33.14 REGEX, +20.42 LOGO, +2.26 CLEVR. Giving the LLM raw Stitch abstractions HURT: -30.60 REGEX, -2.91 CLEVR, -11.11 LOGO. AutoDoc recovered +9.73 REGEX, +2.27 CLEVR, +0.00 LOGO.
limits: Three small synthesis domains. LOGO had semantic errors AutoDoc did not fix.
agent_relevance: Key warning: unnamed chunks can hurt an LLM. Each library entry needs a readable name and usage note.

source: ExpeL (Zhao et al. 2024)
finding: ExpeL extracts natural-language insights and keeps successful trajectories; both are recalled at test time. Insights help reasoning tasks, retrieved trajectories help action tasks.
numbers: Insights-only vs retrieval-only: 36% vs 31% (HotpotQA), 50% vs 55% (ALFWorld). Retrieval-only 40.3% to 54.4% over 1 to 4 experience rounds in one table; ExpeL+Reflexion 54.5% to 60.4%.
limits: Numbers read from text extraction of tables. Which environment each row belongs to was not fully confirmed.
agent_relevance: Two chunk types, abstract rule and concrete episode. Which wins depends on whether the task is knowledge-heavy or action-heavy.

source: Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (Sumers et al. 2024)
finding: CoALA frames LLM agents with working, episodic, semantic and procedural memory. It notes Soar can write new productions into procedural memory, the classic chunking mechanism, and makes a subgoal at an impasse.
numbers: No benchmark numbers (framework paper).
limits: Conceptual, no empirical test.
agent_relevance: Gives the vocabulary: library entries are procedural memory; chunking is writing a production after resolving an impasse.

source: Working memory capacity of ChatGPT: an empirical study (Gong et al. 2024)
finding: ChatGPT shows a working-memory limit on n-back tasks similar to humans: sensitivity d' falls to about 1 at n=3. Adding noise lowers capacity.
numbers: Human norm: sharp drop at n=3. ChatGPT d' near 1 at 3-back. Verbal and spatial variants, with chain-of-thought and noise variants; GPT-4 and several open models tried on the base verbal task.
limits: This is n-back, not span with chunk use. It measures attention-like capacity, not chunk count.
agent_relevance: Do not assume chunking raises usable capacity in LLMs. Measure it before using human limits as design numbers.

source: Gong et al. (2024) Working memory capacity of ChatGPT
finding: Prompt changes (instruction strategies, chain-of-thought) did not remove the capacity limit pattern.
numbers: Authors report the capacity-limit pattern persisted across instruction strategies. Per-strategy d' values not extracted.
limits: Details not extracted.
agent_relevance: Prompting alone does not lift the limit. External memory is needed.

source: Karvonen (2024) Emergent world models and latent variable estimation in chess-playing language models
finding: A GPT trained only on chess game text learns an internal board state that linear probes can read out.
numbers: Legal move rate 99.8% (16-layer) and 99.6% (8-layer). Best probe 99.6% (16-layer trained) versus 74.7% on a randomised-weight model. A second column in the table reads 90.5% for the trained model (metric not verified).
limits: Real human games, not random positions. High score on a randomised model shows many squares are easy (empty).
agent_relevance: Learned stores can hold structure, not only surface chunks. It does not test the random-position contrast.

source: Wenliang et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers: a case study on chess
finding: A 270M-parameter transformer trained on Stockfish labels, with no search, plays at grandmaster level. Memorisation is ruled out for most test boards.
numbers: Lichess blitz Elo 2895 against humans; puzzle Elo up to 2867. Under 1.41% of puzzle boards appear in training. On Chess960 (random back rank) the 9M model dropped from 2054 to 1539 Elo.
limits: Trained on 10M games (15B labels), far more than a human sees. Chess960 test was against bots.
agent_relevance: Echoes Chase-Simon: a huge stored pattern base works until the start layout changes. Supports library value but limited transfer.

source: Search sweep note (this session)
finding: Web search found no arXiv study that gives LLMs the Chase-Simon recall task (meaningful vs random positions) or Miller-style span with chunking. The gap is a finding, but the search was partial.
numbers: No studies found. Search quota ran out; OpenAlex and arXiv APIs were rate limited or empty.
limits: Absence in a partial search is not proof none exists.
agent_relevance: A cheap own experiment is possible: board recall from text for LLMs on game versus random boards.

source: Gobet and Simon (1996) as summarised in search results (random chess positions and skill)
finding: Human boundary condition seen only in a search summary: masters still beat novices on random positions, and CHREST explains this by their larger chunk stock.
numbers: Not read; no figures seen.
limits: Secondhand, page not opened.
agent_relevance: Even random material gets some chunk help, so library gains may leak outside the target class but should be small.

source: Sala and Gobet (2017) meta-analysis of expert memory for random domain material
finding: Seen only as a search listing: the expert advantage on random domain material appears across fields.
numbers: Not read; no figures seen.
limits: Listing only, not opened.
agent_relevance: Human-angle files should record the figures.
